parts.title: Take the Battery Away. Do the Clips STAY or DROP? (Part 1) | Electromagnets
parts.description:
Momo coils a long wire round an iron nail and joins it to a battery. The nail attracts steel clips. Then she takes the battery away. Do the clips stay or drop? Lock in your answer from last time, be the iron nail inside the coil, watch a real scrapyard crane let go of its scrap, spot Momo's dangerous idea, and find out what really makes the nail a magnet. Part 1 of Primary 3 Science, Making and Using Magnets: the electrical method.

In this part:
• Take the battery away: stay or drop? (last episode's dare)
• Be the iron nail in a coil
• Look closer: on and off, and the scrapyard crane
• HOLD ON! Never the wall socket
• Look closer: the battery, the nail, one end or both ends?
• Spot the hidden millipede!

Key words: electrical method, electromagnet, coil.
Watch Part 2: more turns of wire and more batteries for a stronger electromagnet. Last episode: the stroke method.

TheOneApp, Explained: Singapore primary science, made fun. Play along with Pip, Basil and Momo: show fingers to lock in, keep score on your hand, beat the Buddies!

How do you make a magnet you can switch off? P3 Science, Chapter 7, Making and Using Magnets (pp. 115 to 117): coil a long piece of wire around an iron nail, connect the ends of the wires to a battery, and test the iron nail by placing it near some steel clips. A magnet made by this method is called an electromagnet. Take the battery away and the clips drop off. We can increase the strength of an electromagnet by increasing the number of turns of wire around the iron nail. We can also increase the strength of an electromagnet by increasing the number of batteries used. Objects made of iron and steel can be made into magnets using the stroke method or the electrical method. The fifth episode of the Magnets theme. Also fits US NGSS 3-PS2-3 (Grade 3).
Safety and care: Do this only with an adult. Use batteries only, never the wall socket: do not connect the electromagnet to the main electrical supply. Do not keep it connected for too long, because it can get hot, and do not touch the bare ends of the wire. Keep magnets, batteries and nails away from little brothers and sisters. We watch scrapyards from outside. We look at millipedes and crickets, and we do not touch them.
Try it at home: With an adult, coil a long piece of plastic-covered wire neatly round an iron nail, ten times. Join the two bare ends to an AA battery in a battery holder for a moment, and dip the nail's tip into some steel paper clips. Take the battery away: what happens? Then try twenty turns, and then two batteries. Only for a few seconds each time: it gets warm.
A scrapyard crane in an industrial estate, the old electric bell in the school corridor, and Recycling Week at school.
Grade 3 pupils in the US build the same electromagnet with a science kit (NGSS 3-PS2-3): a nail, a coil of wire and a battery.

parts.title: Ten Turns or Twenty? Make the STRONGEST Electromagnet (Part 2) | Electromagnets
parts.description:
Ten turns of wire or twenty? One battery or two? Lock in your answer, be a steel bolt in our mini scrapyard, find out what makes an electromagnet stronger, look inside an old school bell, spot the mistake on Momo's poster, and watch our crane carry the heaviest scrap to the lorry. Part 2 of Primary 3 Science, Making and Using Magnets: the electrical method.

In this part:
• Ten turns or twenty?
• Be a steel bolt
• Look closer: more turns, and the school bell
• Showdown: Momo's poster
• Look closer: one battery or two?
• A chant to remember it all
• Spot the hidden cricket!

Key words: turns of wire, strength, number of batteries.
Watch Part 1: the electrical method, on and off, and staying safe. Next episode: was that test fair?
